extracted.intended_audience: readers of philosophical/personal essays and thinkers interested in moral self-examination
extracted.subtask_description: An introspective, essayistic treatment of moral and psychological topics in the Montaigne tradition: first-person reflections, anecdotes, and maxims about conscience, practice, death, honour, and self-knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience betrays the wicked
rubrics_metrics.description: Conscience produces a displeasure that afflicts us sleeping and waking with tormenting imaginations; it forces men to betray and accuse themselves (e.g., dreams, remorse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and authorities: Lucretius, Apollodorus's dream, Epicurus's remark that no hiding-hole conceals the wicked, Juvenal's line 'Tis the first punishment of sin that no man absolves himself.' Use such examples to show how internal judgment reveals guilt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good conscience gives assurance
rubrics_metrics.description: A good conscience gives greater confidence and assurance; knowledge of one's own will and innocence steadies a man in hazards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Scipio's conduct when accused (refusing to abase himself, redirecting assembly to give thanks, tearing up his accounts rather than submitting them to examination). Use public examples of calm self-possession as evidence of inner innocence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Torture is a trial of patience, not of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The rack and like tortures are dangerous inventions: pain will force false confessions and cannot reliably distinguish truth from falsehood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted maxim: 'Pain will make even the innocent lie.' Use historical trials (Philotas) and common sense: extreme pain induces false statements; many nations regard such torture as horrible and unjust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument alone won't produce action — use makes perfect
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction and argument are insufficient to produce action unless the soul has been practiced and exercised by experience for the intended course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophers seeking excellence purposely exposed themselves to hardships (voluntary poverty, labour, austerities). For training for danger or virtue, cultivate habits by deliberate practice rather than mere study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Death cannot be fully practiced, only approached
rubrics_metrics.description: We can prepare for many hardships by custom, but as to death itself practice can give no full assistance because one can experience it but once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sleep and swoons approximate death; philosophers who sought to 'taste' death found only approximations. Use analogies (sleep resembles death) and near-death anecdotes (Julius Canus, the author's swoon) to justify partial preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Near-death experience reduces dread by approximation
rubrics_metrics.description: Approaching death (swoon, near-fatal accident) can reconcile one to death and lessen fear, because imagination often inflates things beyond their reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's personal accident: swooning, numbness and later pain demonstrated that the imagined terror was often worse than reality. Encourage deliberate exposure or reflection to demystify feared events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speaking of oneself is allowable and useful if impartial and truthful
rubrics_metrics.description: Although custom discourages talking of one's self (to avoid boasting), candid self-examination and reporting one's experience can be valuable; it is a legitimate subject of study and communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defend first-person discourse by analogy to craftsmen who describe their art from their own practice; cite Socrates as example of self-directed teaching. Caveat: keep reports impartial and avoid vanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious and impartial in valuing oneself
rubrics_metrics.description: One should be very cautious how one values oneself and give a true report—speaking less than one is is folly, and speaking more is presumption and often folly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle referenced: undervaluing is cowardice; overvaluing breeds indiscreet self-love. Strive for measured, honest self-assessment rather than flattery or self-deprecation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honour as recompense should be rare and non-monetary
rubrics_metrics.description: True recompense of honour derives its essence from rarity; honours that carry monetary or commonplace benefits are debased and less esteemed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical example: Augustus's sparing distribution of honour; the Order of St. Michael held value because it conferred no material commodity. Recommendation: preserve honours' distinct, noncommercial character to retain dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue loses value when it becomes customary
rubrics_metrics.description: When a virtue or its recompense becomes common practice, it ceases to be a proper recompense — rarity is essential to the dignity of honour and virtue's esteem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Spartan virtues not praised because universal; if an honour is given too liberally it brings it down to nothing. Preserve selectivity to maintain the worth of honour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects (external achievements) indicate fortune, not inner essence
rubrics_metrics.description: External effects and achievements speak more of fortune and circumstance than of a person's inner essence; writing of self aims to expose the essence rather than catalog acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing oneself, emphasize internal dispositions and motives rather than solely external accomplishments or outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bodily motions in swoon are not necessarily evidence of conscious agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Movements and utterances during swoon or near-unconscious states can be automatic sensory responses, not true acts of the self; passions that only touch the 'outward bark' are not ours in full.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite examples: fingers groping, reflexive motions, animals' post-mortem twitching; don't infer full conscious experience from such outward signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: One should not abase oneself to prove innocence
rubrics_metrics.description: A guilty or innocent person's behaviour under accusation can differ: extreme defensiveness or self-abasement is not necessarily proof of innocence; true assurance may manifest as refusal to debase oneself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scipio's responses to accusations (redirecting the crowd, destroying his accounts rather than submitting them) serve as examples of how dignified self-assurance can be a sign of integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination enlarges fears; lived experience often diminishes them
rubrics_metrics.description: Many things seem greater by imagination than they are in effect; experiencing an affliction often reveals it to be less dreadful than anticipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's own recovery from illness and confinement showed imagined suffering was more intense than actual; counsel to temper fear by testing and exposure where possible.
